questions.question: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
questions.explanation: Distance is a scalar (path length); displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors.

questions.question: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Displacement has a magnitude and a direction; the others are scalars.

questions.question: A person walks 6 m east and then 8 m north. The magnitude of their displacement is:
questions.explanation: Displacement = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10 m. Distance walked is 14 m.

questions.question: A car drives 50 m east, then 30 m back west. Its displacement is:
questions.explanation: Displacement = final − initial position = 50 − 30 = 20 m east. Distance is 80 m.

questions.question: An athlete runs once around a 400 m circular track. Distance and displacement are respectively:
questions.explanation: Path length is 400 m; the start and end points coincide, so displacement is 0.

questions.question: Distance is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of displacement.
questions.explanation: Path length ≥ straight-line distance between start and end. Equality when motion is in one direction without reversal.

questions.question: The SI unit of displacement is the ____.
questions.explanation: Displacement has the SI unit of length: metre (m).

questions.question: Average velocity is defined as:
questions.explanation: Average velocity = Δx / Δt — displacement (not distance) divided by time.

questions.question: Average speed is defined as:
questions.explanation: Average speed uses total path length, not displacement.

questions.question: An object travels 100 m in 20 s. Its average speed is:
questions.explanation: Average speed = 100 / 20 = 5 m/s.

questions.question: A car travels at 60 km/h for the first half of a journey and 40 km/h for the second half (equal distances). Its average speed for the trip is:
questions.explanation: For equal distances, average speed = 2 v₁ v₂ / (v₁ + v₂) = 2 × 60 × 40 / (60 + 40) = 4800/100 = 48 km/h.

questions.question: Instantaneous velocity is geometrically interpreted on a position–time graph as:
options: the slope of the tangent at that instant
the slope of the chord between t = 0 and t
questions.answer: the slope of the tangent at that instant
questions.explanation: v(t) = dx/dt = slope of tangent to x–t graph at t.

questions.question: Average speed and the magnitude of average velocity are equal whenever the motion is in one direction throughout.
questions.explanation: For unidirectional motion, distance = |displacement| so the two averages match.

questions.question: The SI unit of velocity is ____.
questions.explanation: Velocity = distance / time; SI: m/s.

questions.question: The SI unit of acceleration is:
questions.explanation: a = Δv/Δt → m/s divided by s → m/s².

questions.question: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of:
questions.explanation: a = dv/dt; the rate of change of velocity (vector quantity).

questions.question: Uniform velocity means:
questions.explanation: Uniform velocity → constant magnitude and direction → acceleration is zero. Options 2 and 3 are equivalent.

questions.question: A car's velocity changes from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 4 s. Its average acceleration is:
Which of the following is TRUE?
options: A body with positive velocity must have positive acceleration.
A body slowing down can have positive or negative acceleration depending on the direction of motion.
Negative velocity always means the body is decelerating.
Acceleration is always in the direction of motion.
questions.answer: A body slowing down can have positive or negative acceleration depending on the direction of motion.
questions.explanation: The signs of v and a are independent. Slowing down means a opposes v in direction; the actual sign depends on which direction is positive.

questions.question: Uniform acceleration means a is constant in magnitude AND direction.
questions.explanation: Uniform = constant; for a vector this means constant magnitude and direction.

questions.question: On a velocity–time graph, the slope at any point equals the ____.
questions.explanation: a = dv/dt = slope of v–t graph.

questions.question: Which kinematic equation does NOT involve t (time) explicitly?
questions.explanation: The third kinematic equation eliminates t between the first two.

questions.question: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s. Its final velocity is:
A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 4 m/s² for 6 s. The distance travelled is:
A car decelerates uniformly from 30 m/s to 10 m/s over a distance of 200 m. The (constant) acceleration is:
questions.explanation: v² = u² + 2as → 100 = 900 + 400a → 400a = −800 → a = −2 m/s². Negative because the car is decelerating.

questions.question: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes to rest in 5 s. Distance covered while braking is:
questions.explanation: Average velocity during uniform deceleration = (20 + 0)/2 = 10 m/s; distance = 10 × 5 = 50 m. (Or use s = ut + ½at² with a = −4 m/s².)

questions.question: A body starts from rest with uniform acceleration. After 4 s its velocity is 16 m/s. The displacement in those 4 s is:
The kinematic equations v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2)at² and v² = u² + 2as require a to be constant.
questions.explanation: These three equations are derived assuming constant a; for varying a, calculus is needed.

questions.question: The kinematic equation that relates v, u, a and s without involving t is v² = u² + ____.
questions.explanation: Third equation of motion.

questions.question: Which of the following situations cannot be solved directly with the standard kinematic equations?
options: A car accelerating uniformly from rest
A ball thrown vertically with initial velocity u (ignoring air resistance)
A car whose acceleration changes with time
questions.answer: A car whose acceleration changes with time
questions.explanation: The kinematic equations assume constant a. A varying a requires calculus (or piecewise application).

questions.question: The acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface is approximately:
questions.explanation: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward; often rounded to 10 m/s² for quick estimates.

questions.question: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m. Time to reach the ground (g = 10 m/s²):
A stone is thrown straight up with u = 20 m/s (g = 10 m/s²). The maximum height it reaches is:
A stone thrown straight up at 20 m/s reaches the highest point. Time of flight back to launch height (g = 10 m/s²):
questions.explanation: Time of flight = 2u/g = 2 × 20 / 10 = 4 s.

questions.question: A ball is thrown upward with initial velocity 30 m/s. After 4 s (g = 10 m/s²), its velocity is:
questions.explanation: v = u − gt = 30 − 10(4) = −10 m/s. Negative means the ball is now moving downward.

questions.question: In free fall (no air resistance), all objects fall with the same acceleration regardless of mass.
questions.explanation: g is independent of mass. The classic Galileo / Apollo-15 hammer-and-feather demonstration.

questions.question: A stone takes 3 s to reach the ground when dropped from a tower (g = 10 m/s²). The height of the tower is ____ m.
On a position–time graph, a horizontal line indicates that the object is:
questions.explanation: Slope is 0, so velocity = 0 — the object is not moving.

questions.question: On a velocity–time graph, the slope equals the:
questions.explanation: a = dv/dt = slope of v–t graph.

questions.question: On a velocity–time graph, the area enclosed under the curve between two times equals the:
questions.explanation: Displacement = ∫v dt = area under v–t graph.

questions.question: A v–t graph is a straight line from (0, 5) to (4, 25) (units: s, m/s). The acceleration is:
A v–t graph is a straight line from (0, 0) to (10, 20) m/s. The displacement during this 10 s is:
questions.explanation: Area under v–t = (1/2) × base × height = (1/2)(10)(20) = 100 m.

questions.question: A v–t graph crosses the time axis at t = 5 s, going from positive v to negative v. What does this indicate?
options: The body comes to rest and stays at rest.
The body reverses its direction of motion at t = 5 s.
questions.answer: The body reverses its direction of motion at t = 5 s.
questions.explanation: v changing sign means the velocity has reversed direction. (The body momentarily has v = 0 at t = 5 s but is not at rest in the sense of permanent rest.)

questions.question: A straight, sloping line on a position–time graph means uniform velocity.
questions.explanation: Constant slope of x–t graph means constant dx/dt = constant velocity.

questions.question: The displacement of a body between two times equals the ____ under its velocity–time graph between those times.
questions.explanation: Displacement = ∫v dt = area under v–t graph.

questions.question: A ball falling freely has its v–t graph as:
options: a straight line of positive slope starting at (0, 0)
a straight line of negative slope starting at (0, u)
questions.answer: a straight line of positive slope starting at (0, 0)
questions.explanation: If the ball is dropped from rest and we take downward as positive, v = gt — a straight line through the origin with slope g.

questions.question: A car starts from rest, accelerates uniformly to 20 m/s in 10 s, then moves at 20 m/s for another 10 s. Its v–t graph is:
options: two straight-line segments — sloped, then horizontal
questions.answer: two straight-line segments — sloped, then horizontal
questions.explanation: Phase 1 (uniform acceleration): straight sloped line from (0,0) to (10, 20). Phase 2 (uniform velocity): horizontal line at v = 20.

questions.question: An object starts at rest and undergoes uniform acceleration. The ratio of distance covered in the first 2 s to that covered in the next 2 s is:
questions.explanation: Distance from 0 to 2 s: (1/2)a(2)² = 2a. Distance from 0 to 4 s: (1/2)a(4)² = 8a. Distance in 2-4 s: 8a − 2a = 6a. Ratio (0 to 2):(2 to 4) = 2a : 6a = 1 : 3.

questions.question: An object moving with constant acceleration covers 20 m in the 3rd second and 28 m in the 5th second. Its acceleration is:
questions.explanation: Distance in n-th second: u + a(n − 1/2). 3rd second: u + 2.5 a = 20. 5th second: u + 4.5 a = 28. Subtract: 2a = 8 → a = 4 m/s².

questions.question: Two stones are dropped from rest, one 1 s after the other. Just as the first hits the ground, the second has fallen 11.25 m (g = 10 m/s²). The height of the cliff is:
questions.explanation: Let t be the time the first stone falls. The second has fallen for (t − 1) seconds: 11.25 = (1/2)(10)(t−1)² → (t−1)² = 2.25 → t−1 = 1.5 → t = 2.5 s. Height of cliff: h = (1/2)(10)(2.5)² = 31.25 m.

questions.question: Why does increasing g (e.g. on a planet with stronger gravity) reduce the time of flight of a vertical throw?
options: Because t_total = 2u/g, larger g means smaller t.
Because larger g causes the projectile to lose energy faster.
Because larger g changes the initial velocity.
It actually increases the time of flight.
questions.answer: Because t_total = 2u/g, larger g means smaller t.
questions.explanation: Time of flight is inversely proportional to g.

questions.question: A body has a v–t graph that is a parabola opening upward. Its acceleration is:
questions.explanation: If v vs t is parabolic upward, the slope (acceleration) keeps increasing. (For uniform acceleration, v vs t is a straight line, not a parabola; x vs t is a parabola for uniform a.)

questions.question: A train moving at 72 km/h decelerates uniformly and stops in 200 m. The deceleration is:
questions.explanation: u = 72 km/h = 20 m/s; v = 0. v² = u² − 2 a s → 0 = 400 − 2 a (200) → a = 1 m/s² (deceleration). Note 72/3.6 = 20 m/s.

questions.question: An object travels the first half of a journey at 60 km/h and the second half at 40 km/h (equal TIMES). Its average speed is:
questions.explanation: Equal time intervals → average speed = (v₁ + v₂)/2 = 50 km/h. (Different from the equal-distance case which gives the harmonic mean 48 km/h.)

questions.question: A bus accelerates from rest at 1 m/s² for 10 s, then moves at constant velocity for another 20 s. The total distance covered is:
questions.explanation: Phase 1: s₁ = (1/2)(1)(10²) = 50 m, ending at v = 10 m/s. Phase 2: s₂ = 10 × 20 = 200 m. Total = 250 m.

questions.question: If a body is at rest at one instant, its acceleration must also be zero at that instant.
questions.explanation: A ball at the top of its trajectory has v = 0 momentarily but a ≠ 0 (gravity is still acting).

questions.question: The first kinematic equation is v = u + ____.
questions.explanation: v = u + at relates velocity to time under constant acceleration.

questions.question: A particle moves with constant velocity. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Both speed and direction may vary.
questions.explanation: Constant velocity → no change → a = 0. Position is changing (linearly with time) unless v = 0.

questions.question: The second equation of motion is:
questions.explanation: Standard form for displacement under uniform acceleration starting from velocity u.

questions.question: A body starting from rest covers 50 m in 10 s under uniform acceleration. Its acceleration is:
At the highest point of a vertical throw, the velocity of the ball is:
questions.explanation: At the apex the ball is momentarily at rest before reversing direction.

questions.question: At the highest point of a vertical throw, the acceleration of the ball is:
questions.explanation: Gravity continues to act regardless of v; a = g, downward, throughout the flight.

questions.question: Which of the following position-time graphs corresponds to uniform acceleration starting from rest?
options: A straight sloping line through the origin
A parabola opening upward, passing through the origin
A parabola opening to the right
questions.answer: A parabola opening upward, passing through the origin
questions.explanation: x = (1/2) a t² is a parabola in t; at t = 0, x = 0.

questions.question: An object has u = 10 m/s, a = 2 m/s², t = 3 s. Find v.
An object has u = 5 m/s, v = 25 m/s, t = 4 s. The displacement is:
If u = 0, a = 2 m/s² and t = 5 s, the displacement is ____ m.
Which of the following can change for an object moving in a straight line at constant SPEED?
questions.explanation: Constant speed only constrains |v|; the body could reverse direction (e.g. ball bouncing back at the same speed). However, for purely 1D smooth motion at constant speed in one direction, only distance changes.

questions.question: A v–t graph for an object thrown straight up and returning to launch height is:
options: a straight line with positive slope
a straight line going from positive v down through 0 to negative v with constant slope = −g
questions.answer: a straight line going from positive v down through 0 to negative v with constant slope = −g
questions.explanation: Throughout the flight a = −g (constant), so v is linear in t with slope −g; v starts at +u, passes 0 at the apex, and becomes negative on the way down.

questions.question: A car uniformly accelerates from rest and covers 80 m in the first 4 s. The distance it covers in the next 4 s is:
When can the magnitude of displacement equal the distance travelled?
options: Only when the motion is along a straight line in a single direction
questions.answer: Only when the motion is along a straight line in a single direction
questions.explanation: For unidirectional straight-line motion path length = straight-line distance; otherwise distance > |displacement|.

questions.question: An object thrown vertically upward has zero acceleration at the highest point of its trajectory.
questions.explanation: Velocity is zero at the apex but acceleration is still g, downward.

questions.question: Distinguish distance from displacement, with one example showing they can differ.
questions.answer: Distance is the total length of the path travelled (a scalar, always non-negative). Displacement is the change in position from start to end (a vector in 1D, with sign). Example: a runner who runs 100 m east and then 60 m west has covered a distance of 160 m, but the displacement is only 40 m east.

questions.question: A car decelerates uniformly from 25 m/s to rest in 10 s. Find (i) the deceleration, (ii) the distance covered before stopping.
A ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of 25 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s². Find (i) the maximum height reached, (ii) the time of flight, (iii) the velocity 1 s after launch.
questions.answer: (i) h_max = u² / (2 g) = 625 / 20 = 31.25 m. (ii) t_total = 2 u / g = 2 × 25 / 10 = 5 s. (iii) v = u − gt = 25 − 10(1) = 15 m/s, still upward.

questions.question: Sketch and describe the v–t graph for a body that (i) accelerates uniformly from rest for 5 s, (ii) moves with uniform velocity for 10 s, then (iii) decelerates uniformly to rest in 5 s.
questions.answer: Phase 1 (0–5 s): straight line from (0, 0) to (5, v_max), slope = +a₁. Phase 2 (5–15 s): horizontal line at v = v_max. Phase 3 (15–20 s): straight line from (15, v_max) to (20, 0), slope = −a₃ (where |a₃| may differ from a₁). The shape is a trapezium. The total displacement equals the area under the trapezium = (1/2)(top + bottom) × height = (1/2)(10 + 20) × v_max = 15 v_max.

questions.question: A train moving at 90 km/h has to stop within 250 m to avoid a signal. Find the deceleration required (assume uniform).
questions.answer: u = 90 km/h = 25 m/s. v = 0. v² = u² + 2 a s → 0 = 625 + 2 a (250) → 500 a = −625 → a = −1.25 m/s². So a deceleration of 1.25 m/s² is required.

questions.question: A car covers the first 30 km of a journey at 60 km/h and the next 30 km at 90 km/h. Find the average speed for the journey.
questions.answer: Time for first half: 30 / 60 = 0.5 h. Time for second half: 30 / 90 = 1/3 h. Total time = 0.5 + 0.333 = 0.833 h. Total distance = 60 km. Average speed = 60 / 0.833 = 72 km/h.

questions.question: (a) State the three kinematic equations of motion for uniform acceleration. (b) A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 4 m/s² for 5 s, then continues at the same velocity for 10 s, then decelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² until it stops. Compute the total displacement.

A stone is dropped from the top of a tower. It takes 4 s to reach the ground. Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance. (a) Find the height of the tower. (b) Find the velocity with which the stone hits the ground. (c) If the stone had been thrown downward with an initial velocity of 5 m/s instead, how long would it have taken to reach the ground?

(a) Explain how the slope of a position–time graph and the area under a velocity–time graph relate to physical quantities. (b) A car's v–t graph rises linearly from (0, 0) to (10, 20) m/s, then is horizontal at 20 m/s from t = 10 s to t = 20 s, then drops linearly to (30, 0). Compute the total distance travelled.
questions.answer: (a) The slope of an x–t graph at any instant equals the instantaneous velocity (v = dx/dt). The slope of a v–t graph at any instant equals the instantaneous acceleration (a = dv/dt). The area under a v–t graph between two times equals the displacement during that interval (∫v dt). (b) The graph is a trapezium with parallel sides 10 s and 30 s, height 20 m/s. Area = (1/2)(10 + 30)(20) = (1/2)(40)(20) = 400 m. Since velocity is positive throughout, distance = displacement = 400 m.

questions.question: Explain why the signs of velocity and acceleration are independent. Give one example of each of the four sign combinations: (+v, +a), (+v, −a), (−v, +a), (−v, −a).
questions.answer: The signs of v and a tell different things: v's sign tells you the current direction of motion, while a's sign tells you whether v is currently increasing or decreasing in the chosen positive direction. They are independent because an object's instantaneous direction of motion does not constrain whether its motion is speeding up or slowing down. Examples (with up = +): (i) +v, +a: ball thrown straight down (v down) on a planet where 'down' is the chosen positive direction. (ii) +v, −a: ball moving up (positive) and decelerating because of gravity (a = −g). (iii) −v, +a: ball moving down (negative) and decelerating (e.g. a parachutist with air resistance pushing up). (iv) −v, −a: ball at the start of a fall — moving down (negative) and accelerating downward (negative).

questions.question: Show that the distance covered by a uniformly accelerated body in the n-th second is given by S_n = u + a(n − 1/2). Use the kinematic equations.
questions.answer: Distance covered in the first n seconds: s_n = u n + (1/2) a n². Distance covered in the first (n−1) seconds: s_(n−1) = u(n−1) + (1/2) a (n−1)². Distance in the n-th second: S_n = s_n − s_(n−1) = u n − u(n−1) + (1/2) a [n² − (n−1)²]. Simplify: u terms → u; the bracket is n² − (n² − 2n + 1) = 2n − 1. So S_n = u + (1/2) a (2n − 1) = u + a (n − 1/2). This is the standard 'distance in the n-th second' formula.

questions.question: Construct a worded problem whose solution requires the third kinematic equation v² = u² + 2as, and solve it.
questions.answer: Sample problem: A car moving at 30 m/s applies brakes producing a uniform deceleration of 5 m/s². How far does the car travel before coming to rest? Solution: u = 30 m/s, v = 0, a = −5 m/s². Apply v² = u² + 2 a s: 0 = 900 + 2(−5) s → 10 s = 900 → s = 90 m. The car stops after 90 m. (Other valid problems: a stone thrown up reaching a given height, a ball rolling down a frictionless ramp from rest, etc.)

questions.question: Sketch the v–t graph for a freely falling body that bounces elastically once off the ground (without losing energy). Take downward as positive.
questions.answer: Phase 1 (free fall, before bounce): v starts at 0 (released from rest) and grows linearly with slope +g until the body hits the ground at time t₁, reaching v = +g t₁. Phase 2 (instantaneous bounce): velocity flips sign discontinuously from +g t₁ to −g t₁ (downward to upward). Phase 3 (going up): v starts at −g t₁ and grows linearly with the same slope +g toward 0; the body reaches the apex at time t₁ after the bounce. The graph thus has two sloping segments of slope +g, with a vertical jump from positive to negative at the bounce. (Alternatively: with up = positive, the slopes are −g and the discontinuity is from negative to positive.)

questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward from the ground with initial velocity u. Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance. (a) Derive expressions for the time to reach the highest point, the maximum height, and the time of flight. (b) Show that the ball's speed when it returns to the launch height is u, and explain why this must be the case using the symmetry of the kinematic equations.
questions.answer: (a) Take up as positive; a = −g = −10 m/s². (i) Time to highest point: at apex v = 0 → 0 = u − g t_up → t_up = u / g. (ii) Maximum height: v² = u² − 2 g h → 0 = u² − 2 g h_max → h_max = u² / (2 g). (iii) Time of flight: by symmetry, t_total = 2 t_up = 2 u / g. (b) Speed on return: at h = 0, applying v² = u² − 2 g (0) = u². So |v| = u. The ball returns with the same speed (but opposite direction). This follows from the symmetry of free fall: the motion under constant gravity has time-reversal symmetry — the descent retraces the ascent in reverse, so the speeds at any given height match. (Energy view: kinetic energy at launch = kinetic energy at return because gravity is conservative and the launch / return heights are equal — but kinematic algebra shows it directly via v² = u²).
